why: It is what the record has for whether a Japanese inn may honestly stand with a stable behind it the way the town maps draw, and it carries two claims of very different weight. The DEFINITION carries the institution: an inn that took a traveler's horse into its keeping was a named kind of place. Only the 1913 sentence carries the arrangement - inn in front, stable behind - and one sentence of fiction is the weakest positional evidence this record uses. Its date is Taisho, after the railway had begun displacing packhorse traffic, so it is an analogue for a premodern arrangement rather than a description of one; and the dictionary's marking it the word's earliest attested example cuts against antiquity, not for it - the compilers found no earlier written use of the sense, so this page does not establish that the word or the arrangement is of the Edo period. It says nothing of a cart yard, a feeding trough, grooms' quarters or any dimension, and nothing of the inn's story count. The wagon-inn analogue on the other side of the same knob owes it nothing. This entry does not rest on the closest physical evidence there is - a national cultural-property entry for an 1801 farmhouse in the mountains of northern Japan registered as a 馬宿, with a two-stall stable and a fodder hearth<!-- Weblio's 馬宿 page carries it, under 奥会津の山村生産用具及び民家（馬宿）, Minamiaizu; not yet fetched by a source-reader --> - and the same kotobank page also carries an encyclopedia passage on a homonymous place, a 馬宿 district in western Japan that was an ancient post station and not an inn, which corroborates nothing here.

It gives, through an encyclopedia's account of the painting, the scene at a Song city gate: wagons, a crowd of donkeys and mules, a few guards - open trodden ground with traffic standing in it, which is the arrangement our gate yards copy. Its limits are that we read the scroll through a tertiary summary rather than the painting or its scholarship; that the article records a scholarly dispute over whether the city is Kaifeng or an idealized city, so the scene carries no measurement; and that the hitching posts and the absence of a fence or a lawn on our gate yards are our reading of the picture, not statements on the cited page.

It says that the Edo intendants of the Kanto lived in Edo and went out to their villages only for land surveys, harvest inspections, tours of inspection and serious incidents, which is the historical form of an official seen rarely in the countryside. The article carries Wikipedia's banner saying it cites no or too few sources, with no citation on this sentence. The sentence concerns the Kanto intendants of the shogunate's own lands in particular, not the daimyo domains. It says those intendants governed through contact with their tetsuke, the staff officers under them, so what was rare was a visit from the intendant himself, not all contact with the state. It gives no count of visits a year, so any frequency is our estimate. It is also the page read for the size of an intendant's staff: about ten shogunal retainers (tetsuki) and a few locally hired clerks (tedai), and at one late-Edo intendancy a single intendant, three tetsuki and ten tedai. Its one scholarly citation (Nakata 2002) supports only its history of how the intendancy became a salaried office, from 1657 through the Kyōhō reforms (1725), and both staff figures are uncited; the Gojō count is given as hearsay ("it is said"). The counts are of officials and clerks only: the article says menial ashigaru and chūgen served beside them, so more hands worked at the office than the figures give. Its two figures do not agree on the mix (about ten tetsuki and a few tedai, against three tetsuki and ten tedai at Gojō). They are for the shogunate's intendancies, which varied in size: one staff ran a district usually of several tens of thousands of koku (Gojō's was 70,000), not a single town. Intendants near the Kantō lived in Edo and came only for surveys, inspections, tours and serious incidents.

It establishes that the chrysanthemum was grown in Japan as a medicine, an ornament and a flower for the altar, which is what a planted field of it could be for. It is the article that Wikipedia itself flags as insufficiently sourced. Its history (the arrival from China, the court festival, the Edo breeding) is footnoted to a 1994 Asahi encyclopedia essay by the horticulturist Tsukamoto Yotaro, but its statement that the flower has been used on altars "since long ago" carries no date and no footnote. It describes breeding and display, not fields, and gives no plot sizes; the only commercial growing it describes is modern (electric lighting, greenhouse cut flowers supplied year-round, dwarfing chemicals) and none of that belongs in the setting.

It gives inn counts for 17 of one highway's 53 stations, the largest and those flanking Hakone, from Miya's 247 down to Fujisawa's 45; the other 36 stations are not given, so 45 is the smallest count listed, not the floor, and the small stations ran below it. Its counts all cite one 2001 popular reference dictionary (Asai Kenji, 『道と路がわかる辞典』), not a period record; the page gives no year for them (they are most likely the shogunate's survey of 1843, late Edo, near the peak of travel). The total of nearly three thousand is hedged "is said", and the counts are the Tokaido's, the busiest highway (Miya's swollen by the Shichiri ferry), so they are an upper range.

It says the Tokugawa stations were given plots along the highway with a fixed frontage division, so that the lots came out even, with entrances bent at a right angle (masugata) and a water channel along both sides or down the middle of the street - the planned side of a road town. It also says most stations were built on existing villages, some joined from several, so the even lots were a re-division along the road rather than a town laid out on open ground, and it gives the bent entrances and channels as things commonly done, not the plan of every station. It is by the leading historian of the subject, and gives no measurements.

It gives the one figure the record found for how much thatch meadow a settlement of a given size kept, and when the grass was cut. It describes the Aso grasslands within living memory (the page says most roofs had gone to tile by the decade from 1955), so its figure is one region's and not a general rule. The page is an unsigned summary (updated 2020) that cites no survey or document for the figure. It gives the figure as a round rule of thumb (a settlement of 50 to 60 households "must secure" 20 to 30 hectares), so it carries an order of magnitude, not a measurement. It describes the Japanese commonly held pampas-grass meadow.

It shows that on the Kiso rivers a bridge of boats was the exception - laid only for the shogun and the Korean embassies, from boats requisitioned from the villages around, while the rivers were ordinarily ferried - and that a few castle towns (Toyama, Morioka, Fukui) kept one standing in place of a ferry, taking it up in floods. It is an article with a banner saying its footnotes are insufficient: its boat counts and river widths carry no footnote, though a Toyama museum catalogue and books on the Korean embassies are among its listed references. China has one paragraph, on the bridge's origin, so it cannot say how common the bridge was on Chinese rivers. Its lead says permanent pontoon bridges were many, so it supports calling the bridge rare only for the Kiso crossings.

It is the top of the Japanese scale - the shogun's school, not a domain's - and records that its hall was rebuilt on the model of the Mito domain's Confucian shrine. It is an article, flagged since 2018 as lacking verifiable sources, and its site areas (12,000, then some 16,000 tsubo) and the hall's 2.5-fold enlargement carry no citation of their own, so we use them for the order of size, not as exact figures. It says nothing of an ordinary domain school's size.

It states which halls a full Japanese temple was held to have, old and Zen. The article itself says the lists vary by sect and era and that the name was used loosely of any large temple; it gives no sizes, and on an ordinary small temple only that Nichiren temples began as one small hall and added buildings over time. It is an article with one reference (the Iwanami Buddhist dictionary, footnoted only for the Zen list); the older list names its Kamakura text but is not cited. Its China section traces the shift from a pagoda-centred to a hall-centred temple but lists no halls.

It is a walled-city temple that survives with its axis and its own bell tower, measured. It is a capital temple founded by a powerful eunuch as his family temple and named by the emperor, so larger and richer than a provincial one: its black glazed-tile roofs are the mark of a Ming imperial or imperially commissioned temple, which a provincial temple would not have. Only its middle range of three survives, and the length, width and area it gives are of that range today, not of the whole original compound. It is an article whose halls and measurements come from the temple's own visitor guide, and the buildings were restored in 1958 and 1986, with new side gates added.

Its rows show the shared washing place as a common thing in town and village alike - Gujo Hachiman's castle-town channels of the 1650s and their kawado, Hirosaki's spring-fed washing places with drinking and washing tanks kept apart, washing spots with rules of use on the hamlet channels of Fuji town in Saga (a row that gives no date), and Omihachiman's piped town water from a parent well. It is a list, compiled no earlier than 1998 from what municipalities reported, uneven row by row, and what it describes is what survives. Its rows date their things unevenly: Gujo's channels to 1652, Hirosaki's Dagi spring to before 1689 but its strict separation of drinking and washing tanks only to the years after the Second World War, and the Saga and Omihachiman rows not at all. So a row shows the form of a practice, not that the form is premodern, unless the row dates it.

It gives the height of the shophouse of South China and Southeast Asia: two or three stories, with the shop below and the family above. It is a short article flagged since 2017 as needing expansion. The sentence we use cites two studies of Singapore (a 2006 Berkeley working paper on Niucheshui and a 1992 Singapore book on public space), not any South Chinese town. Most of what it shows is the colonial-era shophouses of Singapore, Malaysia, Hong Kong and Taiwan, of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, and it credits their narrow plan and five-foot arcade to colonial tax, structural and building rules. So it is late, southern and mostly Southeast Asian evidence for a premodern county town, good for the form of the building and not for a number.

It describes the long-strip allotment: farmhouses along both sides of a road, each with its field and coppice running in an equal strip behind it, 40 ken of frontage by 375 ken of depth in Kamitome. Its limits: it is an encyclopedia stub, and nothing it cites supports the strip layout or its measurements, so it carries the shape and the figures should come from a work that cites a source. It is one planned colony on dry upland, not a paddy village, and a lord's survey rather than a form that grew by itself. Its strip is a colonist's whole allotment of 5 chō (about 5 hectares), coppice included, with houses about 73 m apart, several times an ordinary farm household's holding, so it is not a plot size or house spacing for a paddy village. It says nothing of tenancy. It is a different work from the architectural paper on the same colony's allotments, which the record also cites.

It gives a great city temple's precinct, its count of sub-temples, and the size and setting of its lost main hall. The passages that give these figures carry no footnote of their own (the article's sources are the 1830s Edo meisho zue, a Tokyo National Museum page and a tourist site), so the numbers are the article's and untraced; the 305,000 tsubo (about 100 ha) is the whole temple ground at its late-Edo height, with its shogunal mausolea, sub-temples and groves, not one walled court. A shogunal temple in the capital is at the top of the range, far above a provincial city's.

It carries the treasury, the 713 order, and the lending of donated wealth at a profit, which the record uses for a Chinese temple as an economic house. It is a stub resting on one Japanese article (Hayakawa 1987), and it gives no reason for the 713 order. It does not put the profit-lending in the Three Stages treasury itself, whose gifts it says went to building and repairing temples; it puts that lending in the other schools the scheme spread to, in the temple stores of the late Tang and after. Its one example is a treasury of the capital's great temple (Chang'an, then Luoyang), not a town temple.

It names the scattered, intermixed holding as the long-standing pattern the land reform failed to break. It is a partial extract from the old edition of a modern general encyclopedia, in an entry on a twentieth-century reform. It dates the pattern only as "from of old", and it gives no count of parcels to a household. Its 1.1-hectare average farm is a 1930s figure from after the Meiji land-tax reform, not a premodern household's holding, and is not to be used as one.

It says the name for Zenkoji's gate soba seems to have settled from the density of the soba shops and from worshippers looking for a resting place and a meibutsu, a place's famous specialty - the word used of what a worshipper seeks at a temple's gate. It is an article that Wikipedia itself flags as insufficiently sourced, and the sentence rests on footnotes this project has not read. It speaks of the present-day street in a modern writer's words, hedges the account ("seems to have"), and gives no date for when the word was first used there - so it shows meibutsu is the word used today for what a worshipper seeks at a temple's gate, not that the word was used so in the Edo period.

It states that the shogunate established and kept tree avenues along the Five Highways and other main roads, which bears on what lined a trunk road near a town. The Nikko avenue itself is an exceptional memorial planting; the article does not say how continuous the ordinary highway avenues were, or how far from a town they ran. Its one sentence on the shogunate's avenues cites a popular trivia paperback (ロム・インターナショナル編『道路地図 びっくり!博学知識』, 2005), so it carries only that such avenues existed, not their extent or when they were ordered; a dictionary entry on 並木 (Kotobank) that dates the order to 1604 would be the closer source.

It dates the spread of the earthen storehouse in one town and gives the reasons, which says how far that town's count stands above the ordinary. It is a tourism register's short entry drawing on the town's tourist association and the Edo-period gazetteer Shinpen Aizu Fudoki, not a survey. Its count of about 4,000 is for the whole modern city, rural settlements included, counts the storehouses standing today (brick ones among them, a Meiji-and-later build), and is given only as what is said. The spread it dates begins among the wealthy from 1804-1830, but it reached ordinary houses and farmhouses only after the fire of 1880, in the Meiji era: the count that sets Kitakata apart is mostly post-Edo, and an Edo-period count would have been lower.

It says what a town's kido was for, that a watch house went with it, and that some castle towns (Sendai, Matsuyama) set them only at their entrances and at the line between the samurai and townsman quarters. It is a brief dictionary entry with no sizes and no count.

It says the fair gathered near the temple, first on its religious festivals and later on fixed dates, took on trade, and so became a form of the Chinese market, citing in a footnote a Qing note that a capital temple held one on the ninth of each month. It is an article whose references are mostly popular web pages, and it mixes premodern and modern practice. Its only dated evidence is two period texts quoted in its footnotes, and both are about the capital, Beijing: the Qing note above, and a Ming description of the City God temple's fair, held on the first, fifteenth and twenty-fifth of each month with stalls three li long. So it describes a capital's fairs, not a county town's. It gives no area for a fair's ground, and that stall length is a capital's.

It describes a real Edo-period city fish market sited on a canal bank for the boats, the second case beside Edo's. It is a stub whose account of the market cites nothing (its three notes support side points: a painting of the Tenma market, the prefectural office across the canal, the ward's name), so the move to the canal and the three meetings a day are the article's word, used for the shape and not as a checked figure. It gives the market's site and rhythm, not its buildings. And it describes a larger scale of place than ours: the wholesale fish market of Japan's second city, which took in nearly all the catch shipped from Kyushu, Shikoku and the Inland Sea coasts, with 84 licensed wholesalers by 1772; a smaller city's fish market would meet less often and on a smaller scale.

It measures a real riding ground of the period: about 6 chō (about 650 m) east to west by 30-odd ken (about 55 m) north to south. The article footnotes this figure to the Edo meisho zue, the illustrated gazetteer of Edo published 1834-36, about two centuries after the ground was laid out; the breadth is approximate ("30-odd") and the metric conversions are the article's own. It was the shogunate's ground in the capital, built for its bannermen, so we use it to bound a riding ground's length from above rather than to set it; that a domain's ground was smaller is our reading of scale, not something the article says. The article is mostly about the modern district, and carries a banner saying its sources are insufficient. The gazetteer it cites is public (National Diet Library, NDLJP:1174144/283) and is the closer source for the number.

It says where teahouses gathered - at temple gates, along the highways and at the ends of post towns, and in the busy quarters of the cities - which is where a map puts them. These are dictionary and encyclopedia entries, only two of them signed (Harashima Yoichi in Heibonsha's World Encyclopedia; Tsutsui Koichi and Endo Motoo in Nipponica). They are summaries that give the pattern, with no counts or sizes. They also say that what stood at a gate was often not a building. The first temple-gate tea sellers were peddlers carrying a brazier and kettle on a shoulder pole. The teahouses of temple-gate towns and busy quarters began as reed-screened stalls, and shops in their own buildings came only later.

It places the state granary in the county seat, against the village's own store. Its limits are that it is a short article citing one modern monograph and a dictionary; that its sentence placing the granary "mostly" in the county seat under the magistrate is cited to Robert Marks's study of late-imperial South China, so it most likely describes the Qing system in that region, not every dynasty; and that the article itself says the Ming built no national system of these granaries, so a Ming-modeled county seat need not have one.

It gives the Qing local elementary school for orphaned and poor children, which a court order told every province, prefecture and county to set up, and which was founded by officials, by local donation or by one private person. Its limits are that it is a stub with a banner saying it cites no sources, so its dates and the pupils' ages (six to eleven) are unchecked and serve for the shape of the school, not as figures; that it covers only the Qing, from 1702; and that it says nothing of the school's building or where it stood.

It is the smallest whole domain school read for this record - about 3,089 square meters - and its building list (a hall of letters, classrooms, a book store, sword, jujutsu, spear and archery halls, an office and a guardhouse) names no Confucian shrine, so it is the evidence that a school could go without one. It is one domain building late, on the ground of a converted official residence in the town. It is an article without inline citations. The missing shrine was unusual: the Nagano city history (長野市誌 第四巻, in its section on the founding of the school, 文武学校の設立) names it as what set this school apart from the Ueda, Takato and Takashima domain schools, which had one. So it shows a school could do without a shrine, not that many did. Matsushiro was a domain of 100,000 koku, so its ground is the smallest read here, not the smallest a domain school could be.

It sorts the Edo-period castles without a keep into four kinds - a keep lost and never rebuilt (Edo, Osaka, Kanazawa, Fukui, Saga), a keep base with no keep (Tsu, Akashi, Ako), no keep base and a three-story turret standing in for a keep (Yonezawa, Yamagata, Mito), and neither (Kagoshima, Hitoyoshi) - which makes the keep a form a castle may or may not have. It names examples, not how common each kind was; its only count is 65 keeps standing in 1854. Its section on castles without a keep cites no source. It describes Japan alone, where the keep appears from the 1570s, and says nothing of Chinese walled cities.

It dates the book whose Qingming passage the record quotes, through its preface of 1635. Its limits: a short article flagged for needing citations, for possibly containing original research, and for lacking inline citations - its one footnote supports its Jingwan claim, so the preface date and the authorship rest only on its uncited references (Carpenter 1988, Ledderose 2004); and it names Liu Tong as author while saying Yu Yizheng, a Beijing native, compiled the book and Liu "may have just polished the prose", so the book is better credited to Liu Tong and Yu Yizheng together. It is used only for the book's authorship and the date of its preface.

It gives the year of his Yangtze journey, 1861, which dates the observation of shod cattle in north China that the horseshoe page quotes from him. It is a stub that Wikipedia marks as lacking reliable references and that rests mainly on the 1901 Dictionary of National Biography, and it says nothing of shoeing itself. It dates only his journey up the Yangtze, which went through central and western China, not the north. That the shod cattle were seen in north China in 1861 comes from the quoted passage, not from this page, which can only place the report in the mid-nineteenth-century Qing.

It gives rice's threshold and classes it moderately sensitive, which is the measured fact behind this page's rule that a tannery's brine must not reach the paddy. It is a soil-salinity table and does not draw the field-water distinction this page draws.

It dates the cart inn to the end of the Qing, which places the form before 1912, and says its rooms held long heated platforms sleeping about twenty. It is a short article resting on a 2001 popular history, two provincial newspaper pieces and one untitled reference; it admits the name's first use cannot be dated and puts it only roughly in the late Qing and early Republic; it speaks of one frontier region only; and it gives the form an industrial-era cause - the late-Qing opening of the Changbai mines and animal carts fitted with rubber tires borrowed from the motor car - so the dense string of inns about forty li apart that it describes belongs to the 1900s, not to a premodern road. Its figure of about twenty sleepers to a platform carries no footnote.

It is the one page read that sets a dry field inside the paddy on an alluvial fan, and it dates the practice to about the thirteenth century on the mainstream view. Its limits: a short summary resting on Mizoguchi (2002) and other studies centered on Aichi, whose count comes from the 1884 cadastral maps; and its crops are a short list given as examples - cotton, mulberry and figs "and so on", which it says "varied sharply by era" - so its silence on grain is not evidence that none was grown (in Owari, cotton commonly followed a winter wheat or barley crop on dry fields).

It says what the Okido was, a guarded checkpoint on a highway at the edge of the shogun's capital, beside which the aqueduct's open channel ended and its buried pipes into the city began. It is a short summary resting on one Edo-period guidebook (Edo meisho zue, in a 1927 edition) and two modern local-history books (1998, 2007), so we take from it only the gate's date and purpose. It describes one gate of one exceptional city rather than a general type, and that gate stood on Edo's west side, where the Koshu highway and the aqueduct both came in; it does not support which side of our capital the aqueduct ends on.

It states the bund's purpose - that the water not leak out - and names the bund on the ditch side, which is why a basin on these maps is sealed on every side. A stub whose definitions are uncited, used for the definitions only. It describes today's Japanese paddies: its dimensions (a 300-600mm crown, 1:1 slopes under modern field consolidation) and materials (PVC bund sheets, concrete bund blocks) are modern and are not carried to these maps. Its tie to the premodern era is its Yayoi-Kofun section, cited to two archaeology books, which dates bunded small-plot paddies to the Early Yayoi period.
It gives the regional default this page's windbreaks face - the Siberian High's northwesterly in winter; the continental article gives a different winter direction for China.

It answers a layout question for a capital map: the bureaucracy sits on the ceremonial avenue outside the palace wall rather than inside it, which decides where the ministry compounds are drawn. That particular sentence is flagged in the article as lacking a citation, so we treat the arrangement as a plausible shape to draw rather than as a documented fact.

It gives the form of the towpath - a real riverside way, and the slab-on-piers kind standing just above the water - which is what a towpath on our canal maps is drawn from. Its limits are that it describes a preserved heritage structure as it stands now, whose fabric is later than the institution; that the date, the length and the Marco Polo detail are not on the page and rest on nothing readable, so they stand as guesses.

It tells us the form of the household shrine - a small stone or wooden hokora, almost never a shrine hall - and where it commonly stood, which the page gives as the northwest or the northeast of the plot without preferring either; the page goes on to say that treating the northeast as the unlucky demon gate is a later overlay from Onmyodo and a comparatively recent custom, so our maps take a corner and not a compass rule. Its limits are that it is a summary which Japanese Wikipedia itself flags as under-sourced and possibly original research, a heavier discount than the usual encyclopedia caveat; that it describes a folk custom that varied by region and household, so it gives a common pattern and not a rule; and that it dates none of it, so nothing here fixes the practice to the era our maps depict.

One plain point is taken from it - that a magistracy's halls were ordinary timber buildings that burned and were rebuilt again and again, which is why our administrative compounds are drawn as wooden and replaceable rather than monumental. It stands in because nothing closer could be read on a public page: the encyclopedia, museum and tourism pages about the same building describe only its modern reconstruction, so the count of five fires rests on this page alone, and the page is a commercial listing with no sources of its own and its Japanese rendered into English by this project.

Deciding how many monks a settlement of a given size can hold needs an order of magnitude for the share of a population living in religious orders, and this supplies one attributed to a dynastic record - under half a percent. The limits are real: an imperial count is a count of registered clergy, which is not the same as everyone living in a temple.

It tells us who the clerks of an intendant's office were - mostly the sons of village and town officials, hired from peasants and townsmen versed in rural administration - which is what fills the clerks' quarters on our magistracy plans with the right kind of household; it also gives one establishment, Fukuyama domain's twelve clerks under three intendants, four apiece, with their stipends. Its limits are that it is a thin article whose only citation concerns modern commercial law, so its Edo material is uncited; that a recruitment pattern is not a measurement; and that the one staffing figure is a domain's, not a shogunal intendancy's, so if it is ever used it is used as one example.

A castle in our maps needs a back way out as well as a ceremonial front, and these articles establish the plain vocabulary and the plain geometry - the karamete-mon stands opposite the ote-mon. That is all they establish: they name no particular castle, and they say nothing about the divination or orientation reasoning that might have decided which side was which, so any such reasoning on our maps is ours and not theirs.

We use it for one plain fact: that the kuri is where a temple's monks live, which is what puts the country monk's dwelling on the shrine's own precinct. Its limits are that it is a summary with no measurements, and that it describes the institution in general rather than the village temple in particular.

It states the residence half of this project's householder clergy in the source's own words: a Zhengyi priest does not usually live in a temple though he is normally affiliated with one, and such priests are members of families of hereditary priests serving local communities. That is what puts temple families in ordinary houses around a precinct on these maps rather than in cells inside it. Its limits are that it is an encyclopedia entry read on a mirror rather than in the publisher's own edition, and that, like the Patheos article beside it, it describes China and Taiwan today rather than any premodern century - which bites harder here than a date usually does, because the contemporary Zhengyi clergy's non-residence was shaped by the twentieth century, temples confiscated and the tradition rebuilt from the 1980s around household ritual specialists. The historical form of the claim would want a historian of the Chinese clergy, which this record has not reached.

It states the rule our wayside shrines are placed by, and states it as an organizing idea rather than a list: the deity is enshrined at spatial and social boundaries - a village's entrance and exit, a mountain pass, a crossroads, the foot of a bridge - standing by the roadside as a stone monument or image to ward off epidemics and evil spirits coming from outside. That is the landing, the crossing and the gate our city shrines mark. Its limits are that it is an encyclopedia which carries a sourcing-deficiency notice over the very sections the placement sentence sits in; that it does not put such a shrine at a wellhead, which this record had also claimed. It is a different work from the walking-tour company's English page on the same deity, which the record also cites.

It says what stable manure was made of and how, for the Japanese farm our farmsteads are drawn from, and it places the practice in the premodern centuries our setting takes its models from. Its limits are that it is a source whose own banner asks for better footnoting, resting on three historical dictionary entries it lists but does not quote; that it gives no quantities and says nothing about where on a farmstead the manure was heaped; and that by its own account the practice was declining in the early modern period outside the smaller lowland farms, so it describes a common practice rather than a universal one.

The history dictionary says coarse grain was historically outside the land tax and was grown, mostly on dry and slash-and-burn fields, as the farmers' own food and as a famine crop, especially in mountain areas, and that its share grows the further back one goes; that is the reason a village's rice need not feed it alone. It is a short entry with no quantity, so it supports the practice and not a figure. It is about Japan, where "outside the land tax" means coarse grain was not what the tax was paid in (dry fields were still assessed); in north China millet was itself tax grain, so only the diet point carries to China-modeled places. And it weighs the point toward mountain villages: a lowland rice village leaned on coarse grain less.

It dates the stone guardian pair at ordinary shrines to Edo-period commoner donation. Its limits: a rated good article whose Edo-donation claim is footnoted to specialist works (Uesugi, Fujikura); its one count, about 59% of shrines nationally having a pair, is a present-day figure, not a premodern or village-level one, and it gives no size.

It gives the historical sense of the word: in the shoin style the room or building at a residence's formal entrance, and in the Edo period an entrance with a shikidai. Its limits are that it is a summary, most of it about the modern house, and that the historical sentence rests on two architectural dictionaries it cites rather than on a study of Edo houses.

It sets the big door against the ordinary one and dates the word, which is the one width relation found in plain words: the big door was one wider than half a ken. It is a short, unsigned glossary entry that cites no source: it gives the half-ken sense of the word, and its appearance in writings from about the Nanboku-chō period (the fourteenth century), as what is said, not from a document it names, and "wider than half a ken" is where the word's sense begins, not a measured width of any door, so it bounds the big door from below only. It gives no width for an ordinary door and speaks of farmhouses and townhouses, not warrior residences.

It is the one page read that sets out a court's seating tier by tier and says outright that a magistracy's court was roofed or indoor, which is what the hearing court of our county offices is drawn from. Its limits are that it is a short article, a stub, whose four footnotes all cite one popular book on the truths and fictions of period dramas (Sasama Yoshihiko, 2004), with a scholarly dictionary entry (Andō Yūichirō, 2002) listed but tied to no sentence; that its sentence saying the court was roofed or indoor carries no footnote at all, where its seating and its torture statements cite Sasama; that its plan is of the capital's town magistracy, far grander than a country intendant's office; and that it gives only two measures, a plank verandah of 3 shaku along the front of the officials' rooms with a stair of three steps 1 ken wide at its center, and no size for the court or its gravel floor; its statement that the instruments were for show is hedged as what is thought.
